title: The port that had money to spare
learnerQuestion: Why were Chinese ships calling at a Spanish port on the island of Luzon in 1573, and what did the Spaniards there pay them with?
sensitiveContentNotice: This Story discusses the enslavement and freeing of Chinese people at Manila.

header.whereLine: Ciudad de Manila · island of Luzon

paragraphs.text: Here is the thing about a Spanish port on the far side of the Pacific: by about 1572, Chinese ships were already calling at it.
The Spanish officials' relation says that "a year ago" three ships came to the port from China, and five more to the neighbouring islands.
It also says the Chinese goods sold readily to the Spaniards, "since we who are here have plenty of money".
It does not say what kind of money.
What the Spaniards at Manila paid with, and where it came from, is the Story.
In 1573 this is the Ciudad de Manila, on the island of Luzon.
This name was used in this period; present-day orientation is a toggle above the map, not a substitute for it.
Two ships that sailed from the Philippines on 1 July 1573 reached Acapulco in November 1573. Acapulco is on the World map because that is where those ships came in.
Which jurisdiction Manila lay in has not been researched here, so none is shown and no boundary is drawn.
Here is where it gets interesting.

In December 1573 the Viceroy of New Spain wrote to Felipe II that trade with China would have to be carried on in silver, which the Chinese valued above all else. He doubted the king would agree to send silver out of the realm.
In 1576 Governor Sande wrote that he believed the Chinese preferred to trade with the Spaniards at Manila because of the silver from Mexico and the gold of the islands.
Morga, writing in 1609, said the Chinese traders at Manila were paid in silver and reals, because they wanted neither gold nor other goods.
So the question "what did Manila pay the Chinese with?" turns into "where did the silver come from?" The Spanish writers name Mexico, and by Morga's time Mexico and Peru.
Two things complicate the tidy version.
The first is a hard fact. Spanish officials at Manila wrote that Chinese traders came because some Chinese who had been enslaved there were freed and sent home, and spread word of the settlement.
In the officials' own words, freedom and passage to their own country were given to "some Chinese who were slaves among us".

That is the Spaniards' explanation for why the ships came. On their word, Chinese people had been enslaved at Manila and were freed. The report does not say who they were, how many there were, or what they would say about it.
This pilot has not found an account from any of them.

The second is whose account this pilot draws on. Almost all of it is Spanish: a viceroy, officials at Manila, a governor, Morga, and Manila's citizens, who asked in 1586 that the money "which now the Chinese take" not be sent.
Sande, for his part, complained that the Chinese brought poor silks and took the Spaniards' gold and silver away.

The one source from the Chinese side in this pilot is a record of the Ming court from 1589. In it a Fujian official proposes letting 16 ships go to Luzon, and the Ministry of War answers with a cap of 44 ships for each of the Eastern and Western Oceans.
It is the court's voice, and it reckons ship duties in silver. It is not a merchant's.
This pilot has not yet identified an account by a Chinese merchant, or by anyone living in the Philippine islands in the 1570s; no additional record was identified in this documented search.
What can we say, then? The records agree on one plain thing: money went west from New Spain to Manila.
Governor Sande wrote in 1577 that reals, which are coins, were sent from New Spain every year with the provisions until he came to Manila in 1575, and that none had been sent since.
In 1586 Manila's citizens wrote that large consignments of money from rich men in Mexico pushed up the price of all Chinese goods.
In 1588 Governor Vera wrote that a tax of one per cent had been collected for two years at Manila on the coin brought from New Spain, to help pay for a stone fort.
Morga, writing in 1609, said a "succour" in money was sent every year from the royal chest in New Spain to the royal chest in the Philippines, and that the sum varied with need.
Not all of that money was for the Chinese.
Morga's yearly sum went between two royal chests. It shows money crossing the Pacific; it does not say the money went to Chinese merchants.
The citizens' complaint of 1586 is the one that ties money from Mexico to the price of Chinese goods.

So this Story can say that Spanish writers expected, and later reported, that the Chinese wanted silver; that money went west from New Spain; and that Chinese ships were calling at Manila by about 1572, with the Ming court discussing in 1589 how many might go.
It cannot say how much money, from what year, on which ship, or from which mine.
That is a reading of the records, and it is an interpretation.
Historians of the silver trade explain the trade the same way, by China's demand for silver, and the Claim beneath each sentence says whose voice it rests on.

**Not yet researched.** This pilot holds two Stories, each with its own Connection. The paths that would lead out of here — what came before, what followed, what was happening elsewhere at the same time — have not been researched, so none is offered as a researched path. Acapulco, on the World map, is in view to locate this Story, not to begin another. When a path is researched, it will appear here with its own Claims and Evidence.

warnings.name: Evidence concentrated in colonial Sources
warnings.text: Almost all of the primary documents behind this Story are by Spanish colonial writers (`M-C04`); the one source from the Chinese side is a Ming court record from 1589 about licensing ships and taxing them in silver (`M-C17`), and it is the court's voice, not a merchant's. 28 of 30 supporting citations descend, as recorded, from Spanish colonial authors or colonial administrative records. This tells you whose side of events the evidence comes from. It does not weigh the Story's conclusions.

warnings.name: Some voices missing
warnings.text: An account from the Chinese people enslaved at Manila who were freed, and from Chinese merchants, about why they came and what they were paid: not identified in this documented search (`M-C04`, `M-C17`). Three voices are listed below.
